title: Part 3
text: rot in the corners. Blind spots and perfectly arranged grid-like hallways. He was good at dodging, sure, but even he couldn’t run forever. With the girls keeping a low profile and working on the side generators, there was nobody to peel Herman off on so he could catch a break. So, a hiding spot, then. Lockers were a joke. Too loud. He was moving too fast. The slam would carry down the hallway and paint a red arrow over his position. He would have to duck behind something and pray that the movement wasn’t seen before the Doctor could round a corner. He had seen Nea do it entirely too often, just dipping around something and vanishing into a bush like she had never been there. She made it look so easy — as if the Fog itself wanted her to disappear. How hard could it be? Another burst of static shot overhead — a whipcrack of voltage that sent ceiling tiles rattling in their frames. The air sparked, raw and sharp, and Jake barely had time to twist away as flecks of light burst down onto his shoulders like electric hail. He hissed between his teeth, dropped low, and dove through the nearest doorway just as the next pulse detonated behind him. The world exploded in white light. Tile cracked. Something metal shrieked against the wall. Jake didn’t look. He was already crawling. The room was tight — much smaller than he had hoped — and he slid around the edge of what looked like a drained hydrotherapy basin, ceramic walls chipped, grime-stained. It loomed just barely high enough to offer cover if he stayed low. He dropped flat beside it and pressed himself into the crook where tile met basin, chest flush to the floor, body molded tight to every possible inch of safety. And waited. His breath caught. Footsteps. Slow. Measured. Heavy enough to shake dust from the ceiling. The terror radius set his heart screaming against his ribs, Herman’s presence looming like a wall in the doorway. The sparks that danced across his gear made loud pops as they arced between muscle and the doorframe. One arc leapt sideways and lit up a rusted bar in the hallway. Jake flinched, but only internally. His jaw was locked tight. Eyes wide. Pulse screaming. Heavy breathing, tense with irritation, wafted through the room. Jake could hear every movement. The rasp of fabric, the low exhale through grit teeth, the subtle tick of a voltage regulator resetting. If the Doctor turned just a few degrees— If he spotted a boot edge, or the faint smear of dust where Jake had landed... Jake stared at the crack between basin and wall like it held the only safe geometry left in the universe . He didn’t blink. A slam shattered the stillness — a locker, not even 10 feet away. Metal on metal, loud enough to ring. Jake jerked, breath catching in his throat. The footsteps paused. Then turned. An annoyed snarl. Heavy footfalls out the far door. Silence. His heart rate slowly calmed as the radius passed down the hall. He finally allowed himself a full breath. Jake waited. Three seconds. Five. Counted them out in the gaps between heartbeats. And only then — only then — did he move. His body wasn’t moving right anymore. Twitches sparked randomly through his legs, his back, his side — all of it out of sync with anything he actually told them to do. He could feel everything, still, but it came in broken pieces. Signals half-delivered. Feedback loops without return. His heart had given up on rhythm long ago. It beat now in panicked stutters, sometimes too fast, sometimes too slow, lurching through his chest like a drunk trying to remember the steps to a song no one else could hear. His vision shimmered at the edges. A shape loomed in the doorway, blinking in and out of his vision. Massive. Looming. A silhouette writhing with violet static, jagged edges bleeding into the light. He would have flinched from it if any part of him was obeying. The light shifted, and the figure was gone. One of the Doctor’s echoes , then. Hallucinated fragments. They came more often now. He knew they weren’t real — mostly. But the body didn’t care. Especially because there was no way to tell if it was actually real until the moment passed. He counted a breath. Then another. Every breath came wrong — too shallow, too sharp. He focused on keeping the inhale relatively even, but it kept skipping. Tripping. The oxygen wasn’t landing where it was supposed to. It was making him dizzy, and relatively grateful he was already on the floor. His fingers flexed around the cuff, trying to keep a grip on the chain to ease the cut of metal into skin. The edges of the cuff were cutting deeper now. He couldn’t grip hard enough to make it matter. His shoulder was wrong . Out. He could feel it grinding with any shift of weight. He couldn’t remember when it happened. Just that it had been like this a while now — maybe minutes. Maybe hours. Time was buckling. There was a sound, distant. Footsteps. Leon turned toward it. Or — tried to . The floor didn’t move. The angle stayed the same. That wasn’t right. He tried again. Harder. The world jumped forward slightly, and he realized that he must have blacked out for a moment. Kneeling in front of him, shape fuzzed and backlit — hands on his wrist, voice low and fraying at the edges. “—got them. Leon? Hey. Hey, come on, stay with me, I got the keys—” The world didn’t click into focus so much as smear back toward it. Leon blinked, but the film stayed. His body felt... removed. He knew where it was supposed to be. He just couldn’t get to it properly. Something tugged at the cuff above him. Jake fought with the keyhole, the small piece of metal fumbling in his fingers. The skin beneath the cuff was angry and torn, edges blackened with dried blood and weeping slowly against the metal with every shift. It was being absorbed by what looked like a chunk of an old rag. It seemed that at some point, Leon had tried to insulate the wrist by ramming the rag around it between skin and cuff. The fabric looked charred in spots. It was hard to tell if the effort had helped at all. He winced as the skin seemed to break open more with his fussing, but the more damaged key was refusing to seat properly. Rusted. Swollen. Bits of reddish metal flaked off as he tried to get it into position, the pin of the key threatening to bend under the effort. Frustrated, he slammed it down on a nearby gurney and lined up the second key. Down the hall, a generator flared to life with a roar that scattered nearby crows into a frenzy. Small, rapid footsteps hurried in his direction. Jake was still hunched beside him, trying to coax the second key into the lock. His hands were shaking now — not fear, just urgency; too much adrenaline and too little margin for error. The first key hadn’t made it. This one had to. Meg skidded into the doorway, catching herself just short of a full slide across the dust and broken cement. “We only need one more,” she gasped, hopeful. “It’s going to need to be one of the three.” Jake didn’t even look up. “Help me. Get in here and brace him a bit — he’s pulling the cuff down too hard. I can’t get the lock lined up.” Meg blinked — surprise flashing through the exhaustion. “You found the keys?” “No time. Get him steady.” She dropped to her knees, all motion, all hands. Leon didn’t react at first — just swayed slightly as she caught under his arms, gently lifting his torso up enough to ease the weight off the chain. His eyes fluttered, his head slumping sideways with a relieved sigh as the tension came off the dislocated shoulder. Jake hissed a quiet “C’mon...” through his teeth, twisting the key again. He felt the pin resist, then shift — metal scraping metal — before the cuff clicked open with a tired little pop. He let out a relieved chuckle, pulling the cuff free from the damaged skin. No longer pinned above him, Leon’s arm fell heavily against Meg. The shoulder was at an angry angle, wrist raw and bleeding sluggishly, fierce red marks snaking up the arm and across his neck like lightning. His head lolled against her shoulder, no resistance left to even try lifting it. “Jesus...” Meg breathed, quiet now. Alarm tucked deep behind her voice. “How many times did he even get hit?” Jake was already moving to stabilize him, pushing gear aside to reach Leon’s other side. “I lost track after eight,” he muttered, still rushing. “There were more. I know there were more.” “I heard at least two after we left...” she said, shifting to cradle more of the weight. “Good grief, Leon. How the fuck are you even alive?” His chest hitched a couple of times in what could have been a chuckle, one hand trying to grip at her pant leg to pull himself upright to no success. “’m mag’c.” His head drooped, eyes fluttering lightly, and Jake quickly scooped an arm around his injured side to brace the weight as the two of them fought to get him mobile. “Hey,” Jake said gently, ducking under Leon’s arm to help lift him. “No naps yet, man. We gotta move.” Jake hauled Leon out through the doorway with Meg’s help, dragging him clear of the sparking echo-chamber as fast as they could manage. The Doctor’s footsteps were gone, but Jake didn’t trust the silence. Not with how well the bastard could double back. Leon didn’t fight the movement. Didn’t offer very much help either. Just groaned once — low and thin — as they got him moving, leaning heavily between them as he fought to keep his legs moving. Roughly 4 hallways from that cursed room, his vision started smearing again. His head kept dropping forward, as if he was fighting sleep. He made a soft distressed sound, trying to shift weight to get the others to stop. Just wait for a moment. Let him rest. Stop the world from bleeding color in odd directions. Jake planted a hand on his chest to keep him upright, sharing a look with Meg. “Hey. Stay with me. Talk to me. Are you ok?” He tried... He dragged in a shaking inhale, words delayed, the hallway around him shifting in stuttering lurches. The hallway tilted around him, the lights above pulsing in double-exposure. His legs were still moving, but he couldn’t feel the floor anymore. “I... I don’t... feel—” He swallowed hard, forcing the rest out. “I think I’m— I think—” Another tremor hit — small, sharp — surging through his neck and chest like a loose wire sparking inside him. His breath stuttered. “I—wait— I can’t—” His whole face drained out at once, the sentence caught in a broken half-syllable that never finishes, and in that instant, he dropped, head slumping down, chin hitting chest. Jake and Meg nearly fell under the sudden deadweight as his knees gave out under him, Meg squeaking with surprise as she tried to stand fully upright against the pull. A nearby waiting room would have to serve for a break, and they manhandled Leon down to the floor, leaning him back against a dusty seat that provided at least a bare minimum of cover from being spotted from the doorways. His head lolled back against the seat, unfocused slivers of blue barely visible through lightly twitching eyelids. Meg dropped down into a seat across from him, panting and looking nervously back the way they came, while Jake verified that Leon was in fact still breathing. Other than the stuttered rise and fall of his chest, he was completely out. “Kind of surprised he even made it this far.” Jake sat back against another seat, using his shoulder to keep Leon from sliding off to one side. “No kidding.” Meg watched him for a moment, trying to not focus too hard on the way random muscles seemed to shiver in him. “...if he’s down... now what?” “Fuck,” Jake muttered, scrubbing a hand through his hair. “Okay. Okay, think.” They still had a gen left. The prime triad. Worst possible spot. No cover. No soft choke points. Herman would patrol it hard — like he always did — just waiting for someone dumb enough to risk a touch. If Claudette could solo it, maybe they could run interference. Pull Herman wide and get him chasing. It’s not like he and Meg weren’t fast enough to volley him back and forth. But then what? Even if the last gen popped... Even if the gates opened... Even if Herman didn’t catch them before they reached it... How in the hell were they supposed to carry him? Assuming they could get him semi-alert and mobile again, his shoulder was shot. His legs were unreliable at best. There was no way in hell he was going to make it across the yard, through a gate, into the Fog, and out the other side in this state. And even if they dragged him through... Jake glanced over. The bruises. The scorch marks . This wasn’t a trial injury. It was environmental. Would the Fog even heal it? Passing through the Fog via the gates or hatch had a significantly lower impact on the body than anything else, usually only glossing over whatever they had failed to repair en-route. Survivors had been returning to camp for weeks now with random injuries that were barely scabbed over, provided they didn’t get them from a killer or a hook. He looked at Meg. She looked back. Neither said a word. Leon wheezed softly between them — breath like it was playing tug-of-war with gravity. And they both knew. This wasn’t going to work. They needed another way out. Chapter 6: Bargaining Chip The waiting room was dim, sterile, and still. Just beyond the cracked glass of the entrance, the Fog crept like a living thing, curling and slinking along the floor. The quiet was thick. Unnatural. Claudette found them not long after finishing the generator she'd been working on. There was only one left to go, but she knew she couldn’t head back toward that hallway — not after the screams that had followed her out. Instead, she'd traced the outer ring of rooms, hunting for Meg. She spotted them in a waiting room four hallways over. A quick scan around the area told her Herman hadn’t found them yet. No static buzz. No shadowed figure rounding the corner. Nothing. Ducking quickly inside, her eyes locked on Leon. Relief hit first — he was free. The cuffs were gone. But then the rest of the picture registered, and relief twisted into alarm. He was slumped back against the chairs, barely upright, his legs sprawled on the floor like someone had just dropped him there and walked away. Jake was braced on one side, body curved in to keep Leon from tipping, his full focus on the angry red marks scorched across Leon’s wrist. Every few seconds, Leon’s chest hitched in a shallow, rasping breath. Nothing else moved. Claudette shed her jacket without a word and bunched it behind Leon’s head, trying to cushion the harsh angle where seat met neck. The moment she leaned him back against it, he sighed — small and breathy, but real. It settled something sharp in her chest. "Is he going to be ok, do you think?" Meg looked up from across the room. "He's alive, somehow." Meg was pacing in a tight loop nearby, boots scuffing against the tiled floor, arms crossed so tight it looked like she might snap her own ribs. Every few seconds, she flicked a glance toward the corridor like she expected the Doctor to appear out of nowhere. Claudette dropped to her knees beside the boys, careful and methodical despite the obvious panic in her face. She placed two fingers at Leon’s neck, then moved his chin gently to check for responsiveness. There was a hitch in his breathing, a rattling catch that made her shoulders tense. His eyes were unfocused, pupils blown entirely too wide. If he recognized her at all, it didn’t show. He didn’t seem to be unconscious — more suspended between asleep and catatonic — but at least he didn’t seem to be actively crashing in that exact moment. Small favor from the Fog, she supposed. If they could survive multiple cuts, toxins, and being impaled on hooks with nothing more than a band-aid, maybe something in the Fog was keeping him going too. It was more than she’d expected, honestly. This kind of thing wasn’t her wheelhouse. She could handle bleeding, treat infections, even splint a limb if she had to. But this? This was something else entirely. Still, she was the closest thing they had to a medic. That had to count for something. Right? Her hands trembled as she pulled back, brushing a fleck of ash from his collarbone. “He’s stable. Kind of.” Claudette breathed. “But only just. There’s... not much I can do without real tools. Or meds. Or time. I don’t know if the Fog's going to patch this fully on its own." Meg shook her head. "We can try to carry him to the gate, at least. Hope the transition does enough to stabilize him." Claudette hesitated. “The Fog heals trial injuries. We know that. Bleeding, bruises, broken bones... if it happened as part of the trial, it gets fixed. Mostly. But... this?” She gestured softly to Leon. “This wasn’t one wound. It’s systemic. Burnout. Neurological damage. Maybe cardiac. And it wasn’t even clean — this wasn’t a hook, or a weapon. This was... torture. Layered and prolonged. The Fog might not recognize it as something to fix. If we bring him back through the gate like this...” She didn’t finish the thought. Meg rubbed her face and let out a sharp breath. “So, what are you saying? We just leave him here? ” “ Obviously not.” Claudette snapped at her, “But I’m not seeing a way to get him back to the campfire without risking a complete collapse that we can’t fix. Even if a hatch opened right here so we didn’t have to move him, the Fog would bring him back in who knows what condition. It barely manages to clear normal injuries when we leave. And if we get him back and he dies at camp, then what? There’s no precedent for that! We have no idea what would happen!” She rocked back on her heels, hands clenched in her lap, fighting the sinking dread curling at her edges. “I don’t know what to do here.” Jake had been quiet while the girls spoke, chewing over every word like they might unstick something in his brain. Each option seemed just as bad as the last. The hatch and the gate were both off the table—too risky, too uncertain. Either path meant dragging Leon out of the trial and hoping the Fog did something merciful, but the odds were grim. Claudette was right. The Fog was finicky even on a good day. Unreliable. It barely cleaned up normal wounds. And this? This was a total system failure. Although... His fingers curled tight against his knee, jaw tight as he worked through the other half of the thought — the one he didn’t want to say out loud yet. There was a point where it worked overtime on someone, fixing trial injuries so efficiently that it sometimes would repair damage that even the survivor didn’t know they had. It was relatively consistent. Reliable. A complete rebuild from scratch. Not kind, clearly, but practical — the Entity can’t run a trial if there are no pieces on the board, afterall. His stomach twisted. The logic was sound. But the cost? He dragged a hand down his face. Meg was going to punch him. And Claudette might just join her. He ran the loop again, trying to find another route. A loophole. Anything to avoid the conclusion he kept circling back to. But no matter how many times he ran it, the result was always the same. This was the only option that might work. And it sucked. God, it sucked so bad. Jake exhaled slowly, pushing himself to his feet. His hands were slick, but he wiped them against his jeans like that would steady him. It didn’t. “We do have one more option, here.” Jake looked between them, then down at Leon, avoiding the gaze of the girls. If he didn’t look right at them, maybe he wouldn’t lose his nerve. “If the Entity takes someone as a sacrifice... the Fog has to rebuild them. Completely. It doesn’t have a choice. Otherwise, there’s nothing left to throw into the next trial.” Meg stared at him, appalled. “A hook death ? You’re seriously talking about sacrificing him?” Jake ran a hand through his hair, trying to think. “I mean, do you have a better idea? Hook deaths bring a person back to the campfire a lot more whole than escaping out the gate does half the time. It likely won’t fix everything, but it’s a lot more efficient than anything else we have available right now.” A heavy silence fell between them. Meg stared out the doorway like the wall might offer her a rebuttal, but her jaw stayed locked. Jake crouched beside Leon, studying his face. His skin was pale and blotchy in strange patches. The bruising from the cuff had spread in streaks along the electricity burns. He hadn’t come around, but Jake knew Leon would be on his side here. He was practical, quick to take action once a viable path had shown itself. Claudette chewed her lip nervously, mentally mapping out the area. It was a terrible idea, but then again, so was every other one they had come up with. Plus, Jake’s idea at least had a track record. They had all seen it. The hook deaths were horrible to experience, but you always came back with much less physical injury than if you had just escaped or bled out. It could work. But they would have to haul Leon between the three of them, and the closest hook she could remember was several rooms over with a very angry psychopath on the prowl. "None of us can carry him. Not that far." “Oh, don’t tell me even YOU’RE considering this, now?” Meg turned on her, clearly at the limit of her tolerance. The trial had already gone to hell. Now they were just... sitting in a crumbling waiting room, debating the logistics of killing one of their own like it was a strategy meeting? And worse — Claudette’s lack of outrage was only bolstering Jake. His anxious fidgeting was evolving into measured pacing, thoughts coalescing into something more than just theory. “He’d never make it to a hook, not without help. He can’t walk. Can barely breathe. None of us can move him fast or quiet enough.” “And even if we could, we have no way of getting him up there,” Claudette flashed an apologetic look at Meg. “Besides, as far as we know, survivors can’t sacrifice each other. Probably why the Entity keeps the hooks so high up.” “It has to be a killer. The Doctor would have to do it.” Meg choked back a manic laugh — dry and bitter — at the absolute insanity of it all. Her boots scuffed loudly as she turned back to Jake, arms still tight across her chest. “So, what, we just go up and ask him? Please, mister psycho killer, can you sacrifice our friend to your boss for us real quick? We’re too short to reach the hook ourselves! Yeah, that’ll go over really well for us. I’m sure he will just help us out of the kindness of his twisted little heart and not, you know, put the rest of us through the wringer too .” Jake flinched slightly at her anger. She wasn’t totally off, though. He’d already gone through all of that in his head—and worse. And the solution still sat there like a lead weight on his chest. This was going to be a risk. He inhaled, slow and steady, trying to quiet the hammering in his blood. His voice, when it came, was flat and final. “One of you finish the half-done gen by the central room. The other goes to the exit gate. As soon as it's powered, you leave. Don’t wait for me.” Claudette’s eyes widened. “Jake. No. You saw what he did to Leon. He’s angry . You’ve been his primary target all match. If you go near him—” “That’s exactly why I have to,” his voice was sharper than intended, trying to sound more confident than he felt. “He’s not gonna listen to you. Or Meg. But me? He’s been hunting me since I interrupted his game. That’s leverage.” Meg looked like she was biting her own tongue, trying to resist the urge to explode again. “You think you can get him to agree to help? To just... grow a conscience all of a sudden?” "He doesn’t need a conscience. He just needs a reason." She stared at him, open-mouthed for a second, then threw her hands in the air. “Jake, and I say this with all the love in the world, but that is the stupidest thing you’ve ever said.” “What other option do we have?” he snapped back. “Do you want to drag Leon to the gate and hope the Fog decides he’s worth saving? Do you want to guess what happens to someone who dies outside the trials? You think the campfire’s gonna magically fix this? ” He was breathing hard now. The adrenaline was coming back, his tone rising sharp with the pressure behind his ribs He looked down at his hand — still stained with flecks of key rust, cold against his skin. “He’s been on me all match. Ignoring you two. Testing me. Luring me out. That’s something I can use .” Claudette stepped in again, trying to keep him grounded. “You don’t even know if Herman will agree to anything. He could just kill you. Or both of you.” “I know.” “Jake—” He held up a hand, voice cracking slightly from the strain. “I know. Okay? I know. But we don’t have another play. And you know it.” Before they could argue, before Meg could slap some guilt into him or Claudette could plead for a better answer, Jake turned and started walking. Everything in him wanted to run the other way. But someone had to fix this. And it had to be him. Chapter 7: Terms and Conditions Jake crept from room to room, listening for any sign of Herman’s presence. He didn’t need to be stealthy — not for what he had planned—but he wasn’t in a rush to blow the others’ cover before he even knew if this would work. Deep down, though, he knew that wasn’t the real reason. He was stalling. Dragging his feet, hiding in corners, circling the drain. This was insane , no matter how he looked at it. He had caught the faint edges of the Doctor’s terror radius a few rooms back, hovering just at the perimeter like a rabbit watching the edge of a snare. Close enough to start acclimating. Far enough to pretend he could still back out. Jake ran the options again — third time? fourth? — desperately hoping to find a loophole he’d somehow missed. Some clever workaround. Anything other than this. Because yeah, sure, technically he’d be fine in the end. Just another pop back to the campfire, same as always. But the Doctor was a sadist. And this time , Jake was handing himself over willingly. He wasn’t stupid. He knew exactly what that meant. Somewhere behind him, there was the faintest creak of movement — quiet footsteps echoing his own, far enough back to stay out of sight. One of the girls was trailing him, ready to slip in to help if the deal was accepted. They’d figured out who was running the gate and who was staying, then. Good. Smart of them to keep out of view until the last possible second. If this went sideways, no reason for all three of them to go down together. Jake slowed. Listened. He could still hear Herman pacing in a loose arc — stalking nearby, probably trying to flush them toward the generator hallway. The last three were clustered together, too tempting a target for a killer to ignore. He could keep circling. Keep dancing just out of reach. Or he could suck it up and go. He took one steadying breath, set his jaw, and stepped around the corner — out into the open. Herman was done with this trial. The only thing keeping him from quitting the whole charade outright was the gnawing pressure of the Entity’s eyes still fixed squarely on his spine. He’d had one of the pests locked down — neutralized far more efficiently than just bleeding out in the hallway — but the girls had vanished like smoke, and the one survivor he would have liked to disembowel personally was proving to be the single most aggravating little shit he’d dealt with in weeks. Sabotage at every turn. Flitting through his territory like a cockroach with ADHD. Breaking equipment, baiting chases, mocking him. It was enough to make his static flare just thinking about it.
